Optimize Energy Savings With Networked Lighting Controls

# Driving Deeper Energy Savings With Networked Lighting Controls 

Adding networked lighting controls to LED systems can dramatically increase energy savings, simplify building integration, and unlock incentives that help commercial facilities lower operating costs.

 Published: July 16, 2026 at 12:00 PM ET | Updated: 09/21/2026 

(Photo: Adobe Stock | Kalafoto)

By Stuart Berjansky, DesignLights Consortium

W ith costs on the rise, maximizing energy savings is a top concern in offices, retail spaces, universities, and other commercial facilities. The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported that the commercial sector experienced the largest increase (5.2%) in electricity rates over the first four months of this year compared to the same period in 2025. Against this backdrop, building operators are seeking areas ripe for additional savings. And lighting, the third-largest energy consumer in U.S. commercial buildings, has emerged as a promising candidate.

The transition from legacy lighting technologies to light-emitting diode (LED) fixtures has already made significant energy efficiency inroads. According to a DesignLights Consortium (DLC) analysis of Department of Energy (DOE) data, this change saved commercial and industrial facilities in North America 1,000 terawatt hours of electricity from 2010 to 2022. While impressive, that’s a fraction of the savings facility managers could reap if more LED fixtures were installed with advanced lighting controls.

## The Advantages Of Lighting Controls

A 2020 DLC study showed that adding networked controls to LED lighting projects can boost energy savings by an average of about 50% across various building types. Follow-up research in 2023 illustrated even greater savings opportunities through integration of lighting controls with HVAC — a strategy the study indicated could reduce a building’s HVAC energy usage by 30% and potentially cut whole building energy consumption by up to 20%. 

Despite their inherent savings potential, however, deployment of networked lighting controls (NLC) has been slow. While NLC penetration has expanded in the commercial lighting market somewhat over the past several years, a 2024 DOE report (based on 2020 data) revealed that about 70 percent of LED installations still lacked controls of any kind. 

As a non-profit committed to helping decision makers reduce energy use, carbon emissions, and light pollution through quality lighting, controls, and integrated building systems, the DLC wants to change that narrative. Last month (June 2026), we finalized a new policy designed to make it easier for people who plan and implement lighting projects to choose the right systems for their buildings, and to enable more utility incentives that encourage installation of such systems. 

## Lighting Integration Solutions

Taking effect August 3, the latest version of our NLC Technical Requirements (NLC V5.2) reinforces the role of NLCs as a foundation for deeper energy savings through integration of lighting and other building systems. The timing of these updates dovetails with the replacement of first-generation LEDs in commercial buildings across North America, promoting inclusion of integral controls when new lighting is installed. This strategy ensures that potential controls-driven savings aren’t stranded until the next LED replacement window, which is likely a decade away. NLC V5.2 also coincides with changes manufacturers have implemented to simplify control systems in an effort to grow installations.

Provisions in the new NLC policy will enable greater energy savings and improved building performance through changes that make it easier to find DLC-listed lighting products and control systems that work well together (i.e., are interoperable), and features that emphasize new lighting control system capabilities such as thermostat integration. 

The latter is particularly important for enabling energy-saving system integration in smaller buildings. While integration of lighting and other building systems has been catching on in large buildings, it occurs mainly via Building Automation and Control networks (BACnet), a vendor-neutral data communication protocol standard for smart building automation. This pathway isn’t practical for smaller facilities for a couple of reasons — they lack the economies of scale available in larger buildings and are less likely to have an on-site engineer to maintain a building automation system. A feature in NLC V5.2 that highlights new lighting control system capabilities via thermostats will enhance opportunities for NLC-enabled building system integration in small and medium-sized buildings. 

## Unlock Valuable Incentives 

In buildings of all sizes, realizing the potential savings of NLCs depends largely on whether control systems are properly programmed and how the building operators actually use them. Over the past year, the DLC has worked with other stakeholders to advance an industry standard that promotes consistent system configuration reporting. In practice, this provides greater confidence that installed systems are performing as intended — allowing energy efficiency programs to more easily qualify them for valuable incentives.

The new American National Standards Institute (ANSI)/National Electric Manufacturers Association (NEMA) Standard C137.9 enables accurate project data collection in a standard format — an NLC System Configuration Report. For facility managers, this streamlines the process of applying for and obtaining energy efficiency incentives, as the report facilitates verification of ongoing energy savings resulting from an installed NLC system. 

Already, at least one utility has begun offering a specific incentive for an ANSI/NEMA C137.9 compliant NLC System Configuration Report. Regardless of which party completed the NLC system set up/configuration (i.e., electrical contractors, system integrators, commissioning agents, or distributors), building operators should get accustomed to requesting the NLC Systems Configuration Report to support their rebate applications and to provide them with a simple record of how the NLC system was configured. 

With energy costs top of mind, squeezing all the savings we can out of commercial lighting systems through expanded use of integral controls is a logical goal. By streamlining the rebate eligibility process for NLCs, facilitating the selection of interoperable controls and lighting products, and other policy changes, we can broaden the reach and maximize the potential of this transformative technology.
